$comment: Which capabilities each app has, what the INTENT is for each, and how to detect the truth from the source. Read by scripts/check-parity.mjs, which CI runs. The point is that this file does NOT assert what exists: `intent` is a human decision, `detect` is a pattern, and the script reports what the pattern actually finds. A capability that appears on one platform while `intent` says `parity` turns CI red until someone either builds it on the other side or writes down why not. Drift becomes a decision instead of an accident. Prior art: dashpay/platform's SDK parity manifest, which is the only CI-enforced parity system found in open source (2026-08-22) — theirs hand-audits the statuses, this one derives them.

intents.parity: Both platforms must have it. One-sided is a build failure.
intents.ios-only: Deliberately iOS only. `reason` is required and must name an issue.
intents.android-only: Deliberately Android only. `reason` is required and must name an issue.
intents.neither-yet: Neither has it and that is known. Detecting it on either side is a failure, because it means something shipped without this file being updated.

capabilities.name: camera-capture
capabilities.what: The app opens on a camera and takes the photograph. AGENTS.md: the camera is the entry point.

capabilities.name: gallery-pick
capabilities.reason: #28 — whether the first release has a gallery path at all is an open decision. AGENTS.md discusses the gallery at length, which reads as though one exists.

capabilities.name: exif-gps-read
capabilities.what: Reading the coordinate out of a photograph's EXIF block.

capabilities.name: device-location-fix
capabilities.what: Asking the device for a coordinate when the photo carries none, which on the capture path is always.

capabilities.name: category-picker-from-facts
capabilities.what: The twelve categories read from data/reykjavik-form.json at runtime, never hardcoded.

capabilities.name: relay-send
capabilities.what: Posting the multipart report to our relay. Never to the city (decision 0002).

capabilities.name: relay-host-per-build-type
capabilities.what: The relay host comes from the build type, so a release cannot ship the loopback (#29).

capabilities.name: client-telemetry
capabilities.what: The event stream to POST /api/events, so a field test leaves a timeline.

capabilities.name: telemetry-keeps-a-failed-batch
capabilities.what: A batch the relay did not take goes back in the buffer instead of being discarded (#74). The instrument must not lose data exactly while the failure it exists to measure is happening.

capabilities.name: no-city-endpoint-guard
capabilities.what: A test asserting the app knows no city hostname, path or field name.

capabilities.name: contract-pinned-request-test
capabilities.what: A test pinning the multipart body to data/relay-request.json, so a renamed field fails the build.

capabilities.name: crash-reporting
capabilities.reason: Both platforms report to the borgarland-app Firebase project on the personal Google account, Crashlytics only and no Analytics (#53 for iOS, #58 for Android, decision 0012). Android collects in release only: a debug build is the development loop and its crashes belong in logcat, not in a dashboard that exists to show what happens on somebody else's phone.

capabilities.name: signed-release-pipeline
capabilities.reason: Both platforms build signed on hosted runners with no Mac and no local step (decision 0012). iOS exports a signed .ipa to TestFlight on an ios-v* tag; Android builds a signed APK and AAB on an android-v* tag and verifies the upload certificate against a pinned SHA-256 before publishing, because Play pins that certificate to the package name permanently.

capabilities.name: lint-in-ci
capabilities.reason: #2 named ktlint and Android lint as an acceptance criterion; both now run in .github/workflows/android-ci.yml. iOS has no SwiftLint and no decision has been taken on adding one, so this is one-sided on purpose rather than by neglect. Tracked in #58. The parity check caught this the moment ktlint landed, which is the tool doing its job on its first real change.

capabilities.name: report-id-on-the-wire
capabilities.what: Every report carries its own id, generated by the app and stored by the relay as the row's primary key (#88). Sending the same report twice therefore cannot file it twice: the relay answers a repeat with the row it already has, at 200 rather than 201. It is what makes a double press and a retry the same harmless thing, which neither the app nor the relay can otherwise tell apart.

capabilities.name: relay-answer-in-words
capabilities.what: Every relay outcome is one sentence in Icelandic from data/relay-outcomes.json, with the relay's own body still reachable behind a control the person opens on purpose (#77). worker/tests/outcomes.test.ts holds that file to the relay's own source, so a code with no sentence fails the build rather than reaching somebody as raw JSON.

capabilities.name: location-denial-exit
capabilities.what: A location permission that has been denied for good is told apart from one that has merely not been answered, and the screen offers the only thing that can undo it: a button into system settings (#76). Without the distinction the app offers a retry the system will refuse forever.

capabilities.name: submit-reachable-with-keyboard
capabilities.what: The control that ends the screen stays reachable while the soft keyboard is up (#110). The two platforms answer it with different mechanisms and both count: iOS lets the person put the keyboard down, with scrollDismissesKeyboard and a keyboard toolbar (#79); Android insets the scrolling container so the scroll range grows past the keyboard, with imePadding placed BEFORE verticalScroll as Google's edge-to-edge skill requires. Detected on the mechanism each platform actually uses, because one shared pattern would read as a regression on whichever platform solved it the other way.

capabilities.name: offline-queue
capabilities.what: A report that cannot be sent is written to the phone before the attempt and retried when the app returns to the foreground or the network comes back, until it sends or a person discards it. Deliberately NOT a background upload: nothing here runs while the app is dead, which is why the detect pattern names our own type rather than BGTaskScheduler or a background URLSession. Those would be a different capability and a separate decision.
capabilities.reason: #73 — iOS is the platform in testers' hands, and the first field test lost a report to airplane mode. Android has not been observed failing this way and has no delivery pipeline at all (#58), so building it there now would be untested code on a platform nobody installs. The gap is #2's offline-queue criterion and stays open.

capabilities.name: map-correction
capabilities.reason: #2 — AGENTS.md describes the map in the present tense as a correction surface. It does not exist on either platform.
